title: Reading · Seq 2 Medical vocabulary and terminology

questions.stem: About the root (stem) of a medical term:
options: It gives the term its essential meaning
It is always placed at the end of the word
It can appear at the beginning, middle or end of a word
Every medical term has at least one root

questions.stem: In the course's "tree" image of a medical word:
options: The combining vowel is the trunk
The suffix is the branches and leaves
The prefix is the root system that supports and modifies it
questions.explanation: The trunk (root word) remains the central, defining core.

questions.stem: Which terms keep the combining vowel "o" correctly according to the rules?
questions.explanation: Keep o between two roots and before a suffix starting with a consonant; drop it before a vowel: hepatitis.

questions.stem: Why is there no "o" in hepatitis?
options: The suffix -itis starts with a vowel
The o is only used with prefixes
questions.explanation: Rule 2: suffix starting with a consonant → use o; suffix starting with a vowel → drop o.

options: Two roots can never be joined
It means disease of the lymph glands
When the second root starts with a vowel, the o between roots may be dropped
The word is easier to say without the o
questions.explanation: lymph (clear fluid) + aden (gland) + pathy (disease) — the exception to rule 1.

questions.stem: Match the term to its meaning:
options: arthroplasty — surgical repair of a joint
questions.explanation: cardiogram = recording of the heart's activity; cardiology = study of the heart.

questions.stem: Which suffixes begin with a vowel and are attached without the combining vowel?
questions.explanation: -logy, -gram, -pathy start with a consonant and take the o.

questions.stem: Match the prefix to its meaning:

options: Every medical term must have a prefix
A prefix always means the same thing, whatever word it is attached to
Not all medical terms have a prefix
Changing the prefix changes the meaning even if the root stays the same
questions.explanation: The prefix is a "directional sign" giving specific information about the root.
sub- = below/under; hepat = liver; -ic = pertaining to.
The course insists on "multiple diverticula", not "diverticulums".

questions.stem: Which statements about the history of medical terms are made in the course?
options: Medical terms have not changed since antiquity
Most come from ancient Greek and Latin
Many date back to the 1st century B.C., the time of Hippocrates
Medical language keeps growing (e.g. MRI, ultrasound)
questions.explanation: Traditional terms (carditis, osteotomy) coexist with modern names for tests and treatments.

questions.stem: Match the term to its combined roots or prefix:
questions.explanation: myocardial = pertaining to the heart muscle (myo = muscle); "around the heart" is pericardium.
